summary: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa, the site of ancient Carthage and the birthplace of the 2011 "Arab Spring."

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In 670 the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi founded the city of Kairouan and built its Great Mosque, and from then on Islam took root in Tunisia, with Kairouan becoming the earliest center of Islamic learning in North Africa. From the Middle Ages the Maliki school of Sunnism was followed locally, and the Zitouna Mosque University in Tunis trained large numbers of scholars. After independence in 1956 President Bourguiba pursued secularizing reforms and promulgated the Code of Personal Status banning polygamy, but Islam remains the state religion and the faith of the great majority.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In ancient Roman times Carthage was a major center of North African Christianity, producing church fathers such as Tertullian and Cyprian, but after the Arab conquest of the 7th century Christianity gradually disappeared. During the French protectorate of 1881–1956 large numbers of French, Italian and Maltese immigrants brought Catholicism, and after independence most of them left; in 1964 Tunisia signed an agreement with the Vatican handing over most of the churches to the government. Today's Christians are mostly foreign residents and students and migrants from sub-Saharan Africa.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Other faiths include mainly the long-established Jewish community; the El Ghriba synagogue on the island of Djerba is said to go back more than two thousand years and is one of the oldest Jewish holy sites in North Africa. After the founding of Israel in 1948, most Tunisian Jews moved to Israel and France, and their number fell from about 100,000 to a little over a thousand. It also includes a few people with no religion who do not wish to say so openly.

religion.background: Ancient Tunisia was the site of Carthage, founded by the Phoenicians, and in the Roman period it became a major center of North African Christianity. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century Islam gradually became the mainstream, and Kairouan and Tunis became centers of Islamic learning. There have been Jewish communities in the country since ancient times, and under the French protectorate large numbers of European Catholics also poured in. After independence in 1956 Bourguiba pursued secularizing reforms, and after the Jasmine Revolution of 2011 the role of religion in politics became the focus of social debate.

ranking.name: Tunisian Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic arrived with Islam after the Arab conquest of the 7th century, and in the 11th century large-scale westward movements of Arab nomads such as the Banu Hilal accelerated the Arabization of the countryside. Tunisian Arabic (called "Derja") preserves a Berber substratum and has absorbed a great many loanwords from French, Italian and Turkish, differing greatly from Standard Arabic. It is the mother tongue of almost all citizens, while Standard Arabic is used in formal settings and schools, and French is also widely used in business and higher education.

ranking.name: Berber
ranking.description: Berber is the language of the indigenous peoples of North Africa before the arrival of the Arabs. The process of Arabization has made Berber in Tunisia almost disappear, and it is now preserved only in mountain villages in the south such as Chenini, Douiret and Tamezret and in some villages on the island of Djerba. After the 2011 revolution groups promoting a Berber cultural revival appeared, but it has not yet gained official status.

language.history: The earliest inhabitants of Tunisia spoke Berber; after the Phoenicians founded Carthage in the 9th century BCE they brought Punic, and during Roman rule Latin became the language of the cities. The Arab conquest of the 7th century and the movement of Arab tribes in the 11th century made Arabic the mainstream, and Berber gradually retreated to the southern mountains. Ottoman rule from 1574 to 1881 brought Turkish vocabulary, and the French protectorate of 1881–1956 made French the language of the elite and of education. After independence the government promoted Arabization, but French still holds an important place in business and academia.

ranking.name: Couscous
ranking.description: Coarse wheat semolina is rolled into fine granules, steamed over a stew in a special steamer, and then topped with a fish, lamb or vegetable stew seasoned with tomato and harissa.
ranking.history: Couscous comes from the Berber tradition of North Africa and is documented at the latest in the Middle Ages, a staple shared throughout the Maghreb. The Tunisian version is known for its spiciness and red tomato broth, and the coastal regions also have a distinctive fish couscous. Many families make couscous for Friday gatherings, weddings and festivals, and in 2020 Tunisia, together with Algeria, Morocco and Mauritania, nominated it for UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Brik
ranking.description: A sheet of extremely thin "malsouka" pastry is wrapped around a raw egg, tuna, parsley and capers, folded into a triangle and deep-fried, crisp outside with a half-runny yolk inside.
ranking.history: The name and method of brik come from the Ottoman "börek" (filled pastry), introduced to Tunisia during Ottoman rule from 1574 to 1881, and later the tuna and eggs common locally were added. Taking care not to let the yolk run out when eating brik is regarded as a skill. During Ramadan it is the most common appetizer at the iftar meal, and almost every household makes it.

ranking.name: Lablabi
ranking.description: Stale hard bread is torn into a bowl and topped with a hot chickpea soup seasoned with cumin and garlic, then harissa, olive oil, egg and tuna are added.
ranking.history: Lablabi is a traditional breakfast of the Tunisian working class, a hot and filling meal made from cheap chickpeas and leftover bread. It is especially popular in the working-class districts and around the markets of the capital, Tunis, and in winter mornings people can often be seen queuing at small shops. This soup also reflects a principle of thrift common in Tunisian cooking: not wasting bread, because in Islamic culture bread is regarded as a gift from God.

ranking.name: Shakshuka
ranking.description: Eggs are cracked into a spicy sauce made of tomato, bell pepper, onion, garlic and cumin, covered and cooked until the whites set, and eaten by dipping bread in it.
ranking.history: Tomatoes and chili peppers are native to the Americas and reached North Africa after the 16th century through the trade of Spain and the Ottoman Empire, which provided the basic ingredients of this dish. The name "shakshuka" means "mixture" in Arabic and Berber. In the mid-20th century large numbers of Tunisian and Libyan Jews moved to Israel and brought the dish there, making it a popular breakfast in Israel and across the Middle East.

ranking.name: Harissa
ranking.description: A chili paste made by soaking dried red chilies until soft and pounding them with garlic, coriander seed, caraway and olive oil, fragrant, spicy and rich, used in almost every dish.
ranking.history: Chili peppers are native to the Americas and are generally believed to have arrived during the Spanish occupation of Tunis in the 16th century and then to have been widely grown in Tunisia. Nabeul and the Cap Bon peninsula in the northeast are traditional chili-growing areas, and every late summer households dry chilies on their roofs to prepare the harissa needed for a whole year. In 2022 "Harissa" was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list and is regarded as a symbol of Tunisian food identity.
